title: D & G Stout, Inc. v. Bacardi Imports, Inc.
lead: A distributor gives up an exit opportunity after supplier assurances; an appellate remand leads to trial findings and a measured reliance award.

actors.name: D & G Stout, formerly General Liquors
actors.role: Northern Indiana distributor seeking loss of a foregone business-sale opportunity.

actors.name: David Stout
actors.role: General’s president deciding whether to sell or continue.

actors.name: Bacardi Imports
actors.role: Longstanding at-will supplier whose withdrawal undermined continued operation.

actors.name: National Wine & Spirits
actors.role: Competing distributor negotiating to purchase General’s assets.

actors.name: Hiram Walker and Canandaigua
actors.role: Other lines important to General’s proposed survival plan.

proceedings: The District Court granted Bacardi summary judgment on the at-will-assurance theory.
The Seventh Circuit reversed and remanded for proof of promise, reliance, causation, and loss.
After a bench trial, the District Court awarded the company $510,450 including interest and entered judgment for Bacardi on the Stouts’ separate claims.
limits: The 1991 favorable summary-judgment inferences and the 1992 trial findings are separate stages. The later judgment is reported in the canonical brief, not inferred aftermath. No guaranteed future Bacardi profits were awarded.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent primary-source audit claimed.

sections.title: A consolidating market forces General to choose whether to sell
paragraphs: General Liquors, later D & G Stout, was an Indiana corporation operating in South Bend. For liquor supplier Bacardi Imports, organized outside Indiana and operating primarily from Miami, General had distributed its products in Northern Indiana at will for more than thirty-five years. Indiana distributors declined from roughly twenty in 1980 toward two in 1990. In spring and early summer 1987, Brown-Forman and Jim Beam withdrew, leaving General to explore mergers, acquisition, downsizing, or closure.

President David Stout thought General could remain profitable by keeping Bacardi, Hiram Walker, and Canandaigua and closing Fort Wayne. Bacardi also needed a Southern Indiana distributor after Beck closed and invited General to a July 9 meeting to evaluate candidates and General’s viability. Earlier that day National’s James LaCrosse approached Stout about buying assets, and negotiations began.

sections.title: Assurances accompany the immediate sell-or-continue decision
sections.cue: Which version initially governed judicial review?
paragraphs: The account later viewed favorably to General on summary judgment described Stout disclosing a contemplated sale and Bacardi emphatically promising to stay, without a duration. National and General negotiated for about two weeks, while Bacardi remained in frequent contact. By July 22–23 the financial terms were settled. On that record, Stout sought another assurance, received an unequivocal commitment, and told Bacardi he would reject National and continue.

General rejected the offer July 23. Bacardi decided that afternoon to transfer its line, told General July 30, and chose statewide distribution. Hiram Walker withdrew by August 3 because it doubted General could survive without Bacardi; employees left for the remaining distributors, including National. General reopened negotiations in a weaker position, agreed August 14, and closed August 28. The appellate record described a price $550,000 below July’s proposal. These favorable assumptions framed the appeal; the later trial refined important details.

sections.title: The first judge treats at-will status as fatal to reliance
sections.cue: Why did the Seventh Circuit distinguish the claimed loss from future profits?
paragraphs: General sued Bacardi in Indiana federal court under diversity, seeking loss in sale value through promissory estoppel. Judge Miller granted summary judgment because the open-ended at-will assurance did not support the claimed reliance under Indiana law. Both sides accepted that law.

Cudahy, joined by Posner and Flaum, applied Indiana’s Section 90 principle: a promise inducing foreseeable action or forbearance can warrant enforcement necessary to avoid injustice, with relief tailored accordingly. At-will status supplied no fixed future term or guaranteed stream of Bacardi profits, but did not necessarily defeat reliance costs.

The court compared indefinite employment promises, where no future wage term is guaranteed but moving costs or wages surrendered in preparation may be protected. General sought an existing, priced sale opportunity lost by choosing continued operation. National already sold a competing rum and assumed it would not retain Bacardi, so the decline reflected lost bargaining leverage and a going-concern alternative, not simply capitalization of future Bacardi earnings.

The favorable record made an immediate withdrawal’s consequences foreseeable. The reasonable reliance period, promise, causation, and amount nevertheless required trial. On January 31, 1991, the Seventh Circuit reversed and remanded rather than finding liability conclusively.

sections.title: The bench trial finds a conditional promise and objective foreseeability
sections.cue: How did the actual findings differ from the appellate assumptions?
paragraphs: On remand Judge Miller made Rule 52(a) findings after trial. Bacardi promised continuation while General met sales expectations and market conditions stayed stable. It repeatedly reaffirmed and encouraged continued operation but lacked actual knowledge of the specific National negotiations. Stout had decided to reject the July offer before the final July 23 call. Those findings differed from the summary-judgment version without eliminating the applicable legal rule.

The trial record also refined the earlier line losses. Rather than the appellate description of more than half of gross sales, Brown-Forman and Jim Beam comprised eleven and thirteen percent of General’s liquor business; revenues fell from $32.5 million to $19 million. Bacardi knew the account’s importance to survival in the consolidating market and objectively should have anticipated continued operation and surrendered exit opportunities. The court found actual, reasonable, definite, substantial reliance despite lack of notice of this particular negotiation.

sections.title: The award isolates proven reliance losses
sections.cue: What amounts were and were not recovered?
paragraphs: Trial evidence valued July’s proposal at $3.109 million and August’s sale at $1.956 million, with General retaining furniture, equipment, and Fort Wayne property. The court allowed $103,050 net loss on retained personal property, $250,000 inventory loss, $5,000 receivables, and $36,000 South Bend real estate, totaling $394,050. Fort Wayne carrying costs were excluded because that property had been marketed before Bacardi’s promise and costs would arise either way.

Five years of eight-percent simple prejudgment interest applied to the $291,000 portion calculable without discretionary valuation, adding $116,400. Judgment for D & G Stout totaled $510,450. Bacardi received judgment on David and Georgia Stout’s separate claims. The final result compensated proven changed-position losses, not an assumed perpetual distributorship or all differences between the headline sale prices.
